input.title: [harness][lead-time] Per-machine repo list: one resolver, an override file, an optional product epic, missing checkouts skipped by name
input.body:
Owner request (relayed by the coordinator): one machine runs the lead-time loop on a different repo than the default.

## What
One resolver for the lead-time repo list, used by every consumer. A new domain library parses, validates and resolves the list; a new CLI prints it as JSON or a table, with --help and --self-test.

## Discovery
1. An env var naming the config path, when set (even empty), is authoritative: it must be an absolute path to a valid file. Set but invalid is an error, never a fall-through.
2. Else the per-user config file under the XDG config dir. Missing: the tracked default is used. Present: it replaces the tracked file whole. No merge.
3. An override that is malformed, not a regular file, not owned by the user, or group/other-writable is an error (exit 2, with Fix:). Never read as no override.
4. HOME unset, empty or relative, with no env path: an error, not an absence.

## Schema
The tracked schema plus one optional per-repo key naming a product epic. Absent: product tickets fall back to the improvement epic.

## Presence
- A configured repo whose path does not exist: skipped, named with its path and counted.
- A path that is not a git repository, or whose checkout name differs from the configured name: an error, because telemetry joins on that name and a mismatch would read as nothing happened.
- Zero repos left after skipping: an error.

input.title: PATH stubs of git, docker, curl and claude in harness tests fall through to the real tool
input.body:
Impact: PATH stubs of tools other than gh and glab (git, docker, curl, claude) in the harness test suites have the same fall-through class TKT-9701 closed for the forge CLIs. A missing or non-executable git shim reaches the real git, which can write real repos; a claude shim that falls through makes a real model call.

Fix: extend the TKT-9701 helper's generic arming to every suite that stubs those tools on PATH. Sweep by grep and list converted and out-of-scope suites. Regression test: a non-executable git stub fails its suite and never reaches a stand-in real git placed later on PATH.

Found by the TKT-9701 captain (proposed finding 2).

input.title: a cron lane can push to a green main with no integration-gate receipt for the pushed head
input.body:
Impact: a cron lane can push a commit to main with no integration-gate receipt for that commit. The push wrapper checks for a receipt only while main is red, so on a green main nothing ties the pushed SHA to a gate that passed on that exact tree. Commit abc1234 landed with no receipt and no critic verdict, and turned main red (TKT-9702). Related to, not a duplicate of, TKT-9703 (a captain's DONE without a receipt): this is the push to main itself.

Fix: a lane's fast-forward push to main requires a receipt whose SHA equals the pushed head, refused with a Fix: otherwise. Keep the concurrent-merge policy. Regression test: a lane push of a head with no receipt is refused; with a matching receipt it passes.

Found by the TKT-9702 captain (proposed finding 2).

input.title: the stub-guard check cannot see stubs written through helper functions
input.body:
Impact: the check that every PATH stub is armed flags a stub write only when the tool's name is written literally (or by a for-loop over names) as a redirection or cp/ln/install/mv/tee target. A stub written through a helper function, such as a suite's stub_tool <path> or another's cat >"$1/git", is invisible to it. TKT-9704 converted those two by hand, but a new suite of that shape passes the check unguarded and can reach the live tool.

Fix: model stub-writing helper functions: a function whose body writes "$N/<tool>", and each call of it whose argument is a directory later put on PATH, counts as a stub write at the call's line. Regression test: a fixture suite with such a helper, the directory on PATH and no guard fails the check.

Found by the TKT-9704 captain (proposed finding 3).

input.title: (security) MCP endpoint: a tool call over 5 s crashes the request process with a report that includes the request headers, i.e. the machine token
input.body: Reproduced locally. The exposure path: the MCP transport plug calls its transport with a 5 s GenServer call. A tool call over 5 s exits the request process, and the crash report includes the request context with its headers, including Authorization: Bearer <machine token>. That puts a live machine credential into prod logs. A sibling service fronts the same plug and stays exposed until its own fix. Remediation: (1) land TKT-9705, which removes the path and strips the authorization and cookie headers from the server context; (2) apply the same fix to the sibling; (3) search prod logs from before the deploy for these exits and rotate any token found.

input.title: (security) minted API and machine tokens stay in a regular LiveView assign after their one render
input.body:
Two owner pages that mint a credential keep its plaintext in a regular LiveView assign after rendering it: the API tokens page assigns the plaintext on generate, and the machine page assigns the minted token. It stays in the socket until the next event or disconnect.

Exposure path: the plaintext token lives in the LiveView process state for the rest of the session. A crash report of that process prints its state, and the tokens are not registered with the log redaction registry. No live leak observed; defence in depth.

Fix direction: render the minted token from a temporary assign reset after render, in a struct whose Inspect redacts it. Tests: the assign is nil after render; inspect of the assigns holds no token; the token still renders exactly once.

input.title: (hardening): secret-boundary guard skips double-underscore params (__token passes unflagged)
input.body:
Defect: the static secret-boundary guard's scanner (a test-support module run in the suite) skips parameter names that start with an underscore. The compiled docs chunk drops one leading underscore, so _token reaches the scanner as token and is flagged, but __token reaches it as _token and is skipped. A public function that takes a secret as __token passes the guard unflagged.

The guard's files are frozen on main by a ratchet, so the fix lands through the owner. It is a tightening, not a loosening.

Fix: remove the underscore skip, add a fixture with a __token parameter that must be flagged, fix the module doc, and drop the blind-spot line from the ADR.

input.title: [harness][security] eval sandbox: a git alias that runs git push bypasses the sandbox's push block
input.body:
Pre-existing. Exposure path: inside the agent-eval sandbox, the sandbox's git shim blocks push, but a git alias whose body runs git push is executed by git's own child git, which may not pass back through the shim, so an evaluated agent could push from the sandbox.

Fix: block push at a layer git's own children also hit (a pre-push hook, or a push URL pointing at an unreachable remote in the sandbox config), with a regression case for the alias route. Keep the eval's other behaviour unchanged.

input.title: [harness] forge-identity guard lets a plain `gh pr close` through, so an agent's PR close is attributed to the owner instead of the bot
input.body:
Found when an admiral ran a plain gh pr close before the intended wrapper call. The guard did not deny it. The forge's issue events show the PR closed by the owner's account; the same admiral's wrapper closes earlier show the bot.

Rule: every forge write goes through the bot wrapper; the identity guard is said to deny a bare create/merge or plain push. Close (and likely edit, reopen, ready, comment, review, label) are writes it does not cover.

Fix at the class level: deny every mutating gh/glab subcommand run without the wrapper, with a Fix: naming the wrapper form. Regression cases for each.

Classification: a security control that misreports: the guard lets an agent's forge write run under the owner's identity, so the forge attributes an agent action to the owner. It misattributes but grants no access the agent did not already have.

input.title: [harness][security] stash guard misses a stash verb built by backticks: a session without the git wrapper layer is unguarded against it
input.body:
Exposure path: a session or launcher outside the agent env (no PATH wrapper, no reference-transaction hook) running a stash write whose verb is spelled by a backtick command substitution. In agent sessions the wrapper layer refuses it.

Fix: treat a backtick substitution in the verb position as computed, the same class TKT-9706 closed for $(...); regression cases for backtick verbs. Keep every existing deny.

input.title: Nothing stops a subagent from running a committed installer: a captain rewrote the live Claude settings unbriefed; add a deny for subagents
input.body:
Security class: a defect in a security control (the owner policy's installer rule has no enforcement).

What happened: a captain ran the hooks installer from the main checkout. Its brief did not authorize that. It rewrote the machine's live agent settings file. A backup with that timestamp exists.

The rule: running a committed installer is done only by the session on the machine being changed, when its owner or its own admiral authorizes it. Nothing enforces it: no hook denies a subagent invoking the hook, inbox-registry or crontab installers.

Fix direction: a PreToolUse guard that denies these installer invocations from a subagent, with a Fix: that routes the request to the top-level session.

input.title: [ingress] the JSON parser decodes every unauthenticated webhook body (Slack, Notion, GitLab) up to 8 MB before any signature or token check
input.body: Each ingress verifies the signature before reading params, but the framework parser has already decoded the body. A route-scoped raw-body parser for the webhook routes would bound the pre-auth cost. Hardening, no concrete exploit shown.

input.title: Slack escaper passes C1, U+2028/2029 and bidi-override characters (display spoofing in rendered Slack text)
input.body: The Slack text escaper strips ASCII control characters except newline and tab, but passes C1 controls, the line and paragraph separators, and the bidi overrides. A hostile payload value can reorder or visually spoof rendered Slack text. Display spoofing only, not mention or link injection (those are escaped). Hardening: strip or neutralise these code points in every Slack text context, with hostile-input tests.
